generation.hypothesis: A deep neural network potential–based molecular dynamics framework can precisely capture the melting behavior, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloy carbonitrides by resolving atomistic interactions that include nonlinear hybridization effects between metal d-electrons and nonmetal s,p-electrons.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy carbonitrides, for example (TiZrTaHfNb)CₓN₁₋ₓ alloys with variable nitrogen content.
generation.intervention: Simulate the material under gradual heating and cooling at constant pressure using molecular dynamics driven by a deep neural network potential calibrated to replicate DFT-level atomic interactions.
generation.conditions: Temperature varied over a range encompassing the melting transition (approximately 3000–4000 K) and compositions covering from pure carbide to mixed carbonitrides; constant pressure conditions are maintained to mimic experimental environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomistic bonding mediated via strong hybrid bonds between metal d-electrons and non-metal s,p-electrons, including the contribution of C ≡ N triple bonds, which induce nonlinear enhancements in thermal properties.
generation.mechanism: The neural network potential, trained on DFT data, captures subtle changes in bonding and structural disorder as the system transitions from a solid to a liquid state. It quantifies the latent heat effects by resolving energetic differences and structural rearrangements at melting, thus enabling determination of both enthalpic and entropic contributions alongside volume changes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Melting temperature predictions with an error margin of ±30 K, and accurate determination of enthalpy and entropy of fusion and associated volume changes. The method is expected to reveal a nonlinear increase in melting temperature with increasing nitrogen content, consistent with atomistic bond hybridization effects.
generation.baseline: Traditional methods such as DFT calculations and vibrational/mechanical models (Lindemann and Born criteria) that, although accurate for Gibbs free energies and solid-state stability, do not directly simulate homogeneous melt nucleation and detailed liquid state properties.
generation.boundary: The method is tailored to high-entropy alloy systems where similar bonding characteristics (hybridization between metal and nonmetal orbitals) exist; its applicability may be limited when dealing with materials having fundamentally different bonding environments or phase transition mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The accuracy relies critically on the quality and representativeness of the DFT data used for training the neural network potential. Extrapolation to compositions or temperature regimes not well captured during training may reduce predictive reliability.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of controlled molecular dynamics simulations on high-entropy alloy carbonitrides with varying nitrogen fractions. Compare the computed melting temperature, latent heat (fusion enthalpy), fusion entropy, and volume change at melting against experimental measurements obtained via differential scanning calorimetry and dilatometry.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted melting temperatures deviate by more than ±30 K or if the calculated fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, or volume changes show significant discrepancies (beyond experimental uncertainty) compared to measured values across a range of compositions, then the hypothesis that the deep neural network potential framework accurately predicts these properties is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
The melting temperature is a crucial property of materials that determines their potential applications in different industrial fields. In this study, we used a deep neural network potential to describe the structure of high-entropy (TiZrTaHfNb)CxN1−x carbonitrides (HECN) in both solid and liquid states. This approach allows us to predict heating and cooling temperatures depending on the nitrogen content to determine the melting temperature and analyze structure changes from atomistic point of view. A steady increase in nitrogen content leads to increasing melting temperature, with a maximum approaching for 25% of nitrogen in the HECN. A careful analysis of pair correlations, together with calculations of entropy in the considered liquid phases of HECNs allows us to explain the origin of the nonlinear enhancement of the melting temperature with increasing nitrogen content. The maximum melting temperature of 3580 ± 30 K belongs to (TiZrTaHfNb)C0.75N0.25 composition. The improved melting behavior of high-entropy compounds by the addition of nitrogen provides a promising way towards modification of thermal properties of functional and constructional materials.
